newsitem.title: UK: Man held after N.Ireland hospital shooting.
newsitem.headline: Man held after N.Ireland hospital shooting.

text.p: Northern Ireland detectives investigating the IRA shooting of a police officer in a Belfast children's hospital said on Saturday they had arrested a man.
Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said Friday's shooting, in which a bulllet penetrated an empty baby incubator, posed a problem for Irish republicans.
"The use of lethal force in a children's hospital a few days before Christmas by an IRA unit creates a credibility problem for the whole Republican movement."

Bruton added: "If, for instance, a similar operation to last night's one was carried out two years ago in a children's hospital in Sarajevo, rather than in Belfast, world public opinion would demand that the perpetrators and directors of it be made account for themselves before the (international war crimes) tribunal in The Hague."
Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, said the shooting was "a matter of regret for me", but he stopped short of condemning it.
United States congressman Joseph Kennedy said the attack ran counter to pledges he had received from Adams during a visit to Northern Ireland.
"I was given assurances by Gerry Adams just two days ago that there was a de facto ceasefire in existence," the Massachusetts Democrat said.

The shooting of the police officer, a bodyguard for a prominent Protestant politician visiting his ill seven-year-old son, sparked fears that pro-British Loyalist milita will end their two-year old truce.
Police said a man was being questioned in connection with the attack after having been arrested late on Friday.
"We can confirm that a car which may have been used in the shooting incident has been recovered and a man is assisting our inquiries," said a police spokesman.
The incident was the first IRA shooting attack since the guerrillas ended their truce last February.
The bodyguard was slightly wounded when he was shot in a corridor while politician Nigel Dodds and his wife were with their son in an intensive care unit.
The IRA denied it intended to assassinate Dodds, a member of the Protestant, pro-British Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).
David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force, said the IRA was intent on provoking an end to the Loyalist militias' ceasefire.
"My belief is that it is an attempt to provoke Loyalists to retaliate. My fear is that it is more likely than not that they will succeed," Ervine told Reuters.
"It is obvious to loyalism that the IRA is cranking up its war machine," said Ervine, who helped broker the truce by Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain.
Britain and Ireland say Sinn Fein will not have a place in talks until the IRA calls a fresh ceasefire.
